extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, disciplinary counsel, and USPTO Office of Enrollment & Discipline staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria the USPTO applies when deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state disciplinary adjudication of a patent practitioner. Covers statutory/regulatory exceptions, burden of proof, due process requirements, preemption, and sanctioning principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal-discipline exceptions under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: [T]he USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process; (ii) there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject; (iii) the imposition of the same ... by the Office would result in a grave injustice; or (iv) any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four statutory/regulatory exceptions are the exclusive bases for refusing to impose identical reciprocal discipline; the practitioner must meet one by clear and convincing evidence. The text is applied strictly and is the starting point for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent attorney bears the burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements (the exceptions in § 11.24(d)(1)) precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts and the USPTO apply a narrow standard; the respondent must produce clear and convincing evidence of a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the exceptions — mere disagreement with the state outcome is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling v. Radford presumption and narrow standard of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Selling v. Radford, state disciplinary adjudication creates a federal-level presumption that reciprocal discipline is proper; the Director is not sitting as a court of review to discover errors in the state proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO's review is limited — it looks only for the specified defects (due process deprivation, infirmity of proof, grave injustice, or lack of public discipline). Deference is given to the state adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process requirements in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner. In disciplinary proceedings, due process is satisfied by reasonable notice of charges, representation by counsel, opportunity to present evidence, testify, cross-examine witnesses, and make argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities include Mathews v. Eldridge, In re Ruffalo, In re Squire, and In re Zdravkovich. Informal grievance-committee procedures that provide materials considered and an opportunity to respond in writing can satisfy due process; the absence of a particular form of discovery or attendance at an initial grievance committee session does not automatically constitute deprivation of due process unless the respondent shows clear and convincing prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption test for federal patent law vs. state disciplinary authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal patent law preempts state law only when federal patent law 'creates the cause of action' or when a plaintiff's 'right to relief necessarily depends on resolution of a substantial question of federal patent law' (Christianson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the state disciplinary action is predicated on violations of state law (e.g., failure to communicate, conduct prejudicial to administration of justice) rather than on federal patent law, preemption is not established. The mere involvement of patent matters does not grant special protection from state discipline (Kroll v. Finnerty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of USPTO authority versus state regulation of law practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications and procedures for admitting persons to practice before the PTO, and to suspend or exclude patent practitioners from practicing before the PTO; but USPTO regulations disavow preemption of each State's authority to regulate the practice of law except as necessary for PTO objectives (37 C.F.R. § 10.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means states remain able to discipline attorneys for misconduct under state law even when the conduct relates to patent practice, provided the state action does not intrude on the PTO's exclusive admission/suspension authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave-injustice analysis for resisting reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent may attempt to show that imposition of identical discipline by the Office would result in a 'grave injustice'; the analysis focuses on whether the severity of the original sanction 'fits' the misconduct (i.e., whether the original penalty was so ill-fitted to the misconduct that reciprocal discipline would be unjust).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look at whether the state punishment was within the appropriate range of sanctions. Public reprimand is a lesser penalty and is generally appropriate where misconduct violates ethical standards but is not serious enough for suspension/disbarment. Grave-injustice claims require clear and convincing evidence that the sanction was outside acceptable bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity-of-proof standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail under the infirmity-of-proof exception, a respondent must show such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the state adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high bar — the Office requires convincing evidence that the underlying proof was so defective the result cannot be accepted as final. Mere disagreements about weight of evidence will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of consent to discipline on due-process/grave-injustice claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent who consents to a judgment (e.g., agrees to a Conditional Guilty Plea for Consent Judgment and stipulated participation in proceedings) cannot later successfully claim deprivation of due process or that reciprocal discipline would be a grave injustice based on the same proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record of participation and assent undercuts claims that procedural defects deprived the respondent of notice or opportunity; failure to seek further appeal or review weighs against relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific ethical rule violations relied upon in state discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of state-rule misconduct supporting discipline: Florida Rule 4-1.4 (failure to communicate) and Florida Rule 4-8.4(d) (conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice, including through disparagement of others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office may impose reciprocal discipline based on state findings of such rule violations when they concern conduct that is within the state's disciplinary authority and the reciprocal-discipline exceptions are not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural consequences and remedies following USPTO final order
rubrics_metrics.description: When reciprocal discipline is imposed, the Office will reprimand and the OED Director shall publish a Notice of Reprimand in the Official Gazette; disciplinary decisions are publicly available in the OED Reading Room; review of the final decision may be had by petition to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.57(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the administrative/publication and judicial-review procedures that follow a final USPTO disciplinary order.
